name: Neurorealism
statement: Neuroscience language, and pictures of the brain, are said to make an explanation look more credible than the same explanation without them.
meaning: Racine, Bar-Ilan and Illes coined the term for something they saw in newspapers, not in a laboratory. Their subject was coverage that presents an fMRI result as uncritically real, objective or effective, grounded in the belief that a scan is visual proof of brain activity. The experimental literature that grew around the word tests two claims that are usually cited as one. The pictorial claim is that a scan image beside a news article raises how sound its reasoning looks. The verbal claim is that a sentence of brain talk inside an explanation raises how satisfying it feels. Each has its own 2008 paper, and the two have come apart under replication.

origin.who: Eric Racine, Ofek Bar-Ilan and Judy Illes
origin.note: Their paper is a content analysis of 132 non-redundant press articles published between January 1991 and June 2004, 79 from general sources and 53 from specialised ones. They spell the term neuro-realism and set it beside two others they name in the same paper, neuro-essentialism and neuro-policy. No experiment appears in it. The measurable claim now attached to the word comes from two papers published three years later.

evidence: McCabe and Castel ran three experiments. In the first, 156 Colorado State undergraduates read three fictional articles about brain imaging whose conclusions did not follow from the data, each shown with a brain image, a bar graph or no image. Articles carrying a brain image drew the highest ratings of scientific reasoning, above the control condition, F(1, 155) = 5.87, and above the bar graph, F(1, 155) = 8.38. In the second, 128 undergraduates rated articles with a brain image above the same articles with a topographical map of activation, t(127) = 1.85. In the third, 108 undergraduates from Colorado State and UCLA read a BBC News article headlined 'Brain Scans Can Detect Criminals' and rated their agreement with its conclusion on a four-point scale. Agreement was higher when the brain image was present, F(1, 104) = 4.60. The paper reports that its statistical tests were significant at p < .05. Weisberg, Keil, Goodstein, Rawson and Gray tested the verbal claim on descriptions of 18 psychological phenomena. Each was followed by a real explanation or by a circular restatement, with or without an added sentence of brain talk. Three cognitive neuroscientists had confirmed beforehand that the added sentence contributed nothing. Eighty-one novices rated explanations containing neuroscience as more satisfying, F(1, 79) = 6.5, and the gain fell mainly on the bad explanations, F(1, 79) = 18.8. Twenty-two students in a cognitive neuroscience class showed the same pattern, F(1, 21) = 47.1, and a semester of teaching did not shift it, F(1, 21) = 0.13. Forty-eight neuroscience experts showed no main effect of neuroscience, F(1, 46) = 1.3.

replication.headline: The brain picture does not survive replication and the brain sentence does, a split a meta-analysis of 60 experiments also finds.
replication.detail: Michael, Newman, Vuorre, Cumming and Garry set out to build on McCabe and Castel's third experiment and could not obtain it. They ran 10 experiments instead, 1,971 people who completed every phase, using McCabe and Castel's own materials on paper and online. Nine of the 10 produced a confidence interval spanning zero. Pooling those 10 with two findings from the original data in a random effects model gives a raw difference of 0.07 points on the four-point agreement scale, 95% confidence interval 0.00 to 0.14, z = 1.84, p = .07. They put that against the original raw difference of 0.26, which they read off McCabe and Castel's data, and describe the image as exerting little to no influence. Tau was 0.07 with an interval of 0 to 0.13, so paper and online versions cannot be told apart. Hook and Farah ran three studies on 988 people, showing fictional research descriptions and real news articles with brain scans, bar charts or photographs. They report little evidence of seductive allure and none of a link to dualist beliefs. Schweitzer, Baker and Risko ran five more. Their first four, conceptual and direct replications, found no neuroimage bias; the fifth recovered one when people could compare a neuroimage against another depiction of the same data. The verbal effect has gone the other way. Fernandez-Duque, Evans, Christian and Hodges gave 385 students explanations followed by superfluous information of several kinds. Neuroscience text raised judged argument quality for both good and circular explanations, and adding an fMRI picture on top of that text changed nothing, which they read as a conceptual rather than a pictorial bias. Weisberg, Taylor and Hopkins reproduced the effect across three studies of 322, 255 and 159 subjects. Väth, von Petersdorff, Neumann, Mundry and Fischer preregistered a conceptual replication in 2024. Their classroom study of 887 students contradicted the original, with good explanations lacking brain talk rated highest. Their online study of 430 participants and 1,624 ratings found good explanations rated above bad ones, chi-square = 14.6, df = 1, p < 0.001. Brain talk interacted with expertise, chi-square = 17.0, df = 1, p < 0.001, and the boost sat with the least expert. Bennett and McLaughlin pooled 60 experiments from 28 publications in a random effects meta-analysis. Their abstract reports a mild but highly significant effect with substantial heterogeneity, stronger for within-subjects designs than between-subjects ones, and stronger for text than for brain image stimuli.

study.cite: Michael, R. B., Newman, E. J., Vuorre, M., Cumming, G., & Garry, M. (2013). On the (non)persuasive power of a brain image. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 20(4), 720-725.

limits: No figure sits in the original effect-size field. McCabe and Castel report F ratios and mean-square errors. The two numbers usually quoted for their third experiment, a raw difference of 0.26 points and d = 0.40, are Michael and colleagues' readings of the original raw data. Weisberg and colleagues' condition means are also absent from this page. Their scale runs from minus three to plus three, the extracted text of the paper loses the minus signs, and a mean whose sign cannot be read is not a mean that can be published. The pooled estimate from Bennett and McLaughlin is not given here either. Their article is paywalled and only the abstract could be read, so their subgroup comparisons appear above as their own words rather than as numbers. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and the reference list of Farah and Hook's review turned up no multi-laboratory replication of either 2008 paper. The largest attempt on the image side remains 10 experiments run by one group, and the largest on the language side is a single preregistered online study of 430 people. Both original papers used undergraduate convenience samples. The verbal effect is measured by asking people how satisfying an explanation feels, which is a report about a feeling rather than a test of whether they were misled.
misreadings: The commonest error is to cite Racine, Bar-Ilan and Illes for an experimental result. Their paper counted press articles. Of the 132 they coded, 79% carried an optimistic tone, 16% were balanced and 5% critical, and 67% offered no account of what fMRI can and cannot do. Ethical issues appeared in 7%. That is evidence about journalism, and the word neurorealism describes a way of writing before it describes a way of judging. The second error is to treat the brain image finding as established. Farah and Hook argue that McCabe and Castel's illustrations were not informationally equivalent as claimed. The argument in the text turned on similarity of activation across two tasks. The brain rendering showed the shape and location of the activated areas, while the bar chart showed only total activation in the lobe. On Farah and Hook's reading the image carried more support for the conclusion than the chart did. Michael and colleagues collected the overstatements that followed, including an education journal's claim that brain images make educators and scientists more likely to believe the statements, which is not what McCabe and Castel reported. The third error is to read the verbal effect as being about brains. Hopkins, Weisberg and Taylor found the same preference across several scientific disciplines whenever an explanation added reductive information, meaning reference to smaller components or more basic processes. They conclude that people prefer reductive detail rather than neural detail. Fernandez-Duque and colleagues reach the opposite conclusion from four experiments, finding neuroscience text more alluring than social science text and than material from prestigious hard sciences. The two claims are live against each other. A fourth error is to assume the neuroscience sentence is doing all the work. Weisberg, Taylor and Hopkins found that longer explanations were judged more satisfying, and that length and neuroscience made independent contributions, so part of any effect measured with added text is an effect of added words.
